C005.subject: Asynchronous digital communication (e.g., text, email, messaging apps)
C005.object: the depth of emotional intimacy in close friendships among urban young adults
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Asynchronous digital communication (e.g., text, email, messaging apps) the depth of emotional intimacy in close friendships among urban young adults]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey study tracking self-reported emotional intimacy and communication modality frequency in friendship dyads among urban young adults (ages 18-30) over 2-3 years, controlling for baseline intimacy and offline interaction. — Directly measures changes in intimacy over time as asynchronous digital communication use varies, allowing causal inference and temporal ordering.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental study comparing emotional depth in friendship interactions conducted via asynchronous text vs. synchronous video/voice vs. in-person, using standardized self-disclosure tasks and post-task intimacy scales. — Isolates communication modality as a causal factor, controlling for content and relationship duration, to test whether asynchronous channels specifically reduce intimacy.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing cross-sectional and longitudinal studies on digital communication and friendship quality among young adults, focusing on effect sizes for intimacy outcomes. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess overall direction and strength of the relationship, identifying gaps and moderators (e.g., frequency, platform type, cultural context).

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on urbanized regions

C006.subject: Digital communication technology
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Digital communication technology human social bonding]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal study on social media use and perceived social support (e.g., Pew Research Center data on Facebook and well-being over time) — Provides quantitative, time-series data on whether increased digital communication correlates with changes in self-reported social bonding, controlling for offline interactions.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental study comparing face-to-face vs. video chat vs. text-only interactions on measures of oxytocin release or trust game behavior — Directly tests causal mechanisms of bonding through different communication modalities, addressing whether digital technology can replicate or impair physiological and behavioral markers of social bonding.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of studies on 'social presence' theory and media richness in digital communication — Synthesizes existing theoretical and empirical work to identify boundary conditions (e.g., platform design, user demographics) under which digital communication improves or hinders bonding, resolving disputes in the literature.

qualifier.temporal: since the advent of social media platforms (post-2000s)
qualifier.geographic: global, but predominantly in urbanized regions with high internet penetration

C007.subject: Productivity software with always-on availability features
C007.object: risk of burnout among remote workers
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Productivity software with always-on availability features risk of burnout among remote workers]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal survey study on remote workers' self-reported burnout using standardized instruments (e.g., Maslach Burnout Inventory) correlated with objective metrics of always-on software usage (e.g., log-in frequency, response time to after-hours messages) — Directly tests the hypothesized causal link by measuring both exposure (always-on features) and outcome (burnout) over time, controlling for confounders like workload and job demands.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on technostress and boundary management in remote work, focusing on studies published after 2020 — Synthesizes prior evidence across multiple contexts to assess whether the relationship holds consistently, identifying effect sizes and moderators such as organizational norms or personal coping strategies.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework integrating Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model with affordances of always-on software (e.g., constant connectivity, interruption load) — Provides a mechanistic explanation for how always-on features could increase burnout through heightened job demands and reduced recovery opportunities, guiding hypothesis refinement and future empirical tests.

C008.subject: Human mental health
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Human mental health productivity software]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study tracking mental health metrics (e.g., depression, anxiety, burnout) and productivity software usage (e.g., time-tracking, project management tools) across diverse global workplaces from 2020-2024, with controls for confounding factors like remote work intensity. — Directly tests the net effect hypothesis by analyzing temporal correlations and causal pathways between mental health changes and software engagement, addressing the disputed status with quantitative evidence.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on productivity software interventions (e.g., Pomodoro apps, focus-enhancing tools) and their impact on occupational well-being, published in peer-reviewed journals (e.g., Journal of Occupational Health Psychology) between 2020-2024. — Synthesizes existing empirical findings to determine whether the net effect is positive, negative, or neutral, providing a robust evidence base for the hypothesis given its moderate confidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical framework integrating the Job Demands-Resources model with human-computer interaction principles, modeling how features of productivity software (e.g., notifications, gamification) modulate stress and efficiency in knowledge workers. — Offers mechanistic predictions to guide empirical testing and interpret contradictory results, crucial for resolving the disputed status by clarifying underlying causal mechanisms.

C009.subject: Automation and AI
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Automation and AI wealth inequality, thereby reducing]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of wage and wealth distribution data from OECD countries (2010-2025), focusing on sectors with high automation adoption (e.g., manufacturing, retail) vs. low-automation sectors, controlling for education and policy changes. — Directly tests the temporal and geographic scope of the hypothesis by measuring changes in wealth inequality (e.g., Gini coefficient, top 10% wealth share) alongside automation metrics (robot density, AI patent filings).

[PATH:empirical] Causal inference study using natural experiments (e.g., differential automation exposure across regions or industries due to technological shocks or policy changes) to estimate the effect of automation on wage polarization and capital-labor substitution. — Addresses endogeneity concerns and isolates the causal impact of automation on inequality, distinguishing it from other concurrent trends like globalization or financialization.

[PATH:theoretical] Survey of recent theoretical models (e.g., Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2018; Autor, 2015) that formalize mechanisms linking automation to wealth inequality, including task displacement, skill-biased technical change, and asset ownership concentration. — Provides a structured framework to evaluate whether observed empirical patterns are consistent with the hypothesized causal chain and identifies boundary conditions (e.g., role of complementary policies or labor market institutions).

C010.subject: Human economic security
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Human economic security advancement of automation and AI]

[PATH:empirical] Acemoglu, D., & Restrepo, P. (2020). 'Robots and Jobs: Evidence from US Labor Markets.' Journal of Political Economy, 128(6), 2188-2244. — This study provides direct empirical evidence on the impact of industrial robots on employment and wages in the US, which can help assess whether automation has net negative or positive effects on human economic security since the early 2000s.

[PATH:literature] World Bank (2019). 'World Development Report 2019: The Changing Nature of Work.' Washington, DC: World Bank. — This comprehensive report synthesizes global data and research on how automation and AI affect labor markets, income distribution, and social safety nets, offering a broad evidence base for evaluating net effects on economic security.

[PATH:theoretical] Autor, D. H. (2015). 'Why Are There Still So Many Jobs? The History and Future of Workplace Automation.' Journal of Economic Perspectives, 29(3), 3-30. — This theoretical paper argues that automation historically creates new tasks and jobs, challenging the hypothesis of net negative effects. It provides a framework for testing whether current AI advances similarly offset displacement effects.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on industrialized economies
